summary.title: The Grug Brained Developer
summary.one_liner: A humorous, caveman-voiced collection of software engineering advice on complexity, testing, refactoring, tooling, logging, and API design, told through the persona of a simple "grug" developer.
takeaways: Complexity is the main enemy: say "no" to unnecessary features and abstractions, and wait before factoring code until good cut points emerge.
Favor integration tests as the sweet spot, with few unit tests, a small curated end-to-end suite, minimal mocking, and regression tests for bugs.
Be cautious with big refactors, respect existing code (Chesterton's fence), and use a working demo or prototype to ground big-picture designers.
Invest in tooling (IDE autocomplete, debugger, logging with request IDs and dynamic log levels) and measure real performance before optimizing.
Favor simple, layered APIs and sometimes accept some duplication or explicit code over clever DRY abstractions.
summary.summary: The page is an opinionated essay written in deliberately broken, simplified English from the perspective of a self-described "grug" developer. Each section gives a short rule of thumb on a software topic: complexity, saying no, factoring and cut points, testing strategy (integration over unit tests), refactoring, agile, tooling, types, readability, DRY and separation of concerns, logging, concurrency, optimization, API design, and parsing. It mixes humor with practical advice and references figures such as Chesterton, Rob Pike, Bob Nystrom's Crafting Interpreters, and Lea Verou's graph. The page includes no code beyond small examples and no formal structure.
